items.title: 10 Apple TV Shows That Quietly Became Modern Classics
items.author: Safwan Azeem

items.text:
Apple TV entered the streaming wars in 2019, which is pretty late compared to giants including Netflix and Amazon Prime. The platform had to build itself from scratch without decades of TV history behind it, but that’s what made its rise especially fascinating. Apple TV grew its reputation one series at a time. Some became immediate hits while others took a bit longer to find their audience. However, the common thread was that every show on the streamer knew what it wanted to be.

These titles never chased trends. Instead, they fully committed to their own unique worlds, characters, and ideas, and trusted audiences to follow along. A few years later, that consistency has left Apple TV with an unusually strong catalog of shows that already feel like they will go down in history. Here is a list of 10 such shows on the platform that have quietly become modern classics, not long after they premiered.

10
'Pachinko' (2022–2024)

Image via Apple TV+

Pachinko tells its story across decades, but the way its time periods flow into each other is the heart of the story. The series follows Sunja, played in her younger years by Minha Kim and later in life by Yuh-Jung Youn, who is born in Korea under Japanese colonial rule. Her life changes after she becomes involved with the wealthy and mysterious Hansu (Lee Min-ho). The choices that follow eventually take her to Japan, where she is forced to build a life in a country that often treats Koreans like outsiders. Decades later, her grandson Solomon (Jin Ha) is living a completely different life in 1989 as he works in finance and tries to prove himself in a society his family once struggled to survive in.

Pachinko’s intimate storytelling makes it more than just a historical drama. Sunja and Solomon are separated by generations, but the show constantly reveals how much of his life has been shaped by her decisions. The poverty, discrimination, migration, and compromises that defined Sunja’s generation do not disappear, but just take different forms once the family becomes more successful. The show doesn’t make this contrast feel too on the nose, but quietly demonstrates how progress doesn’t always erase the past. Pachinko is one of Apple TV’s most acclaimed dramas because it unfolds on a massive historical scale, but still feels like a deeply personal family story.

9
'For All Mankind' (2019–2027)

Image via Apple TV

For All Mankind begins by changing one moment in history and then spends the rest of the series exploring the consequences of that one decision. In the show’s version of 1969, the Soviet Union beats the United States to the Moon. This throws NASA into a full-blown crisis and makes the space race far more competitive than it ever became in real life. Astronaut Ed Baldwin (Joel Kinnaman) is among the people caught in that shift, as the United States suddenly has much more to prove and far less room for failure. However, this alternate version of the Apollo era gradually grows into a completely different timeline where the space race never really ends.

For All Mankind is one of Apple TV’s most ambitious shows. Every season jumps forward several years, which keeps the story moving in all sorts of interesting directions. Women enter NASA earlier, permanent bases appear on the Moon, and humans actually start inhabiting Mars instead of just dreaming about it. However, even through all these advancements, the show never puts its primary focus on the technology of it all. Every giant leap into the future affects the characters, their careers, and families. This balance between substance and spectacle gives For All Mankind its staying power. The show keeps asking “what if?” on a massive scale, but always makes the answer feel relatable enough to matter.

8
'Bad Sisters' (2022–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Bad Sisters begins with a funeral where almost nobody seems particularly upset about the man in the coffin. The story is set right after the death of John Paul Williams (Claes Bang), while his wife Grace (Anne-Marie Duff) grieves his loss. Now, it doesn’t take the audience long to learn that Grace’s sisters Eva (Sharon Horgan), Ursula (Eva Birthistle), Bibi (Sarah Greene), and Becka (Eve Hewson) all had plenty of reasons to want their brother-in-law gone. Bad Sisters then moves between the aftermath of his death and the months leading up to it. The premise instantly hooks the viewers in, but instead of a traditional murder mystery, they slowly learn how controlling and cruel John Paul really was, to the point where they understand why the sisters would want him dead.

However, the story is complicated when two insurance investigators begin looking into John Paul’s death and quickly realize that something is not right. This structure makes Bad Sisters impossible to stop watching. The show doesn’t take itself too seriously and uses humor to cushion its dark premise without ever undermining the seriousness of Grace’s situation. The show’s greatest strength is the natural dynamic between the sisters who interrupt each other, make terrible decisions, hold grudges, but still show up for each other no matter what. The mystery keeps things moving, but the real reason to stay is the messy, heartwarming, and occasionally disastrous family dynamic that the Garvey sisters bring to every episode.

7
'Widow's Bay' (2026–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Widow’s Bay is a horror comedy that has mastered the art of balancing the two genres without losing what makes them special. The show follows Mayor Tom Loftis (Matthew Rhys), who is desperate to revive the remote New England island of Widow’s Bay and build a better future for his teenage son. The problem is that the locals wholeheartedly believe that the place is haunted, and what’s worse is that they might actually be right. The island has terrible cell service, almost no modern infrastructure, and old supernatural legends that Tom just keeps dismissing. He actually succeeds in attracting tourists by paying no heed to the residents, but that is exactly when the stories he laughed at start coming true.

Apple TV's Widow’s Bay tells this story by refusing to choose between being funny and truly frightening. One episode can play with haunted-house horror, another can feel closer to a slasher, while later stories dig into the island’s much older history. The show never turns those genres into simple spoofs. The horror hits hard while the comedy comes from Tom and the other residents trying to treat completely ridiculous supernatural events like another local problem that somehow needs fixing. Widow’s Bay’s greatest strength is its setting, which has a unique personality. The deeper the show goes, the more its supernatural elements start to make sense. The series could have survived on its bizarre premise alone, but its real achievement is making viewers want to spend more time with the people trapped inside it.

6
'Pluribus' (2025–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Pluribus completely distorts the idea of what should seem like a utopia, and that is the show’s hook. The series follows novelist Carol Sturka (Rhea Seehorn) after most of humanity is suddenly absorbed into a collective consciousness known as the Joining. The event eradicates all crime from the world; people become endlessly helpful, and it looks like everyone is genuinely happy. However, Carol is one of the handful of people who remain immune, and she is horrified by a world where billions of individuals have essentially become one mind. That makes her an awkward kind of survivor, because unlike most apocalyptic protagonists, she is not fighting people who want to hurt her. She is surrounded by people who want nothing more than to make her happy. That contradiction fuels the show.

The collective offers Carol almost everything she asks for, so resisting them doesn’t even make sense. Through this premise, Pluribus keeps forcing the audience to question whether a peaceful world is still worth wanting if everyone has to surrender their individuality to create it. Carol is also the perfect person to explore that idea because she is stubborn, unhappy, and sometimes difficult to like, yet those imperfections suddenly become proof that she still belongs to herself. The show is deliberately patient about answering its biggest questions and spends long stretches showing Carol test the limits of this strange new world she is suddenly in. That slow pace gives the audience plenty of time to sit with the show’s central dilemma instead of rushing toward an easy answer, which is exactly what a narrative like this requires.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.

💊The Matrix

🔥Mad Max

🌧️Blade Runner

🏜️Dune

🚀Star Wars

TEST YOUR SURVIVAL →

01

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…

Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.

The Resistance, Zion

The Matrix

You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.

You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.

You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.

You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.

The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.

The Wasteland

Mad Max

The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.

You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.

You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.

You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.

In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.

Los Angeles, 2049

Blade Runner

You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.

You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.

In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.

You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.

In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.

Arrakis

Dune

Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.

Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.

You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.

Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.

In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.

You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.

You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.

You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.

In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

5
'Silo' (2023–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Silo builds an entire mystery around the unsettling question of what one would do if everything they knew to be real actually wasn’t. The sci-fi series is set in a massive underground structure where roughly 10,000 people live because the outside world is believed to be toxic and uninhabitable. Nobody knows exactly who built the silo or what happened before people moved underground. All they know is that asking too many questions is dangerous, and anyone who says they want to go outside is allowed to leave but can never return. The story eventually centers on engineer Juliette Nichols (Rebecca Ferguson), who begins investigating a suspicious death and slowly realizes that the rules keeping everyone alive may also be hiding something much bigger.

Silo’s gripping premise treats every piece of information like contraband. Everything Juliette finds out puts her life at risk, but what’s interesting is that she approaches every problem like the engineer that she is. If something does not make sense, she keeps digging until she understands how it works, even if that means inviting danger. Every episode of Silo expands the central character’s investigation to reveal the secrets of this underground community going back centuries. Silo uses every revelation to change the meaning of whatever the audience believed they knew. The series opens with a simple premise that eventually turns into one of TV’s most carefully layered worlds, which is why it deserves to be on this list.

4
'Shrinking' (2023–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Shrinking follows therapist Jimmy Laird (Jason Segel), who is struggling to keep up with work and raise his daughter Alice (Lukita Maxwell) after losing his wife. Eventually, he gets tired of sitting quietly through therapy sessions and starts telling his patients exactly what he thinks they should do, instead of letting them figure things out on their own. That obviously crosses every professional boundary imaginable, but it also creates the show’s central tension, because Jimmy begins changing his patients’ lives while he is still figuring out how to rebuild his own. His colleagues Paul (Harrison Ford) and Gaby (Jessica Williams) become an important part of that process.

At the same time, Shrinking never reduces any of these characters to one-dimensional supporting roles. The show allows Jimmy and everyone else in his life to make terrible decisions, but that messiness is what makes their dilemmas feel extremely real. Jimmy’s healing is uneven and complicated, but the humor in his situation comes from the fact that life keeps moving even when he clearly is not ready for it to. The series follows Ted (Jason Sudeikis), an American football coach who is hired to manage struggling English soccer club AFC Richmond despite knowing almost nothing about the sport. What Ted also doesn’t know is that club owner Rebecca Welton (Hannah Waddingham) hired him specifically to fail as part of her plan to destroy something her ex-husband loves. However, Ted walks into this hostile situation with an almost ridiculous amount of optimism. The clever part is that the show never treats Ted’s kindness as stupidity.

Image via Apple TV

Slow Horses builds its entire premise around failure, but manages to tell an extremely hopeful story. The show follows MI5 agent River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), who is sent to Slough House after a disastrous training exercise nearly ruins his career. The unit is run by the brilliant but extremely rude Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), who is more interested in insulting his team than helping them.

However, this group of rejects seems to have a strange habit of getting pulled into real intelligence operations. What’s interesting, though, is that these situations often prove that they are the only people who can actually see the problem clearly. The agents in Slough House are definitely the underdogs here, but that’s what makes all their wins feel earned. Even Lamb, who looks completely checked out initially, eventually comes through and proves exactly why MI5 has never been able to write him off completely. The series has now grown into one of Apple TV’s longest-running dramas, and the way it continues to work with the same basic idea just goes to show the brilliance of its writing.

'Severance' (2022–Present)

Image via Apple TV

Severance makes office life feel terrifying without changing much about it. The series follows Mark Scout (Adam Scott), an employee at Lumon Industries who has undergone a procedure that completely separates his work memories from his personal ones. His “outie” remembers nothing about the office, while his “innie” knows nothing except the time he spends inside it. That means one version of Mark gets to leave at the end of every shift, while the other effectively exists only to work. However, things start to unravel when Mark and his coworkers Helly (Britt Lower), Dylan (Zach Cherry), and Irving (John Turturro) begin questioning what Lumon actually wants from them.

Severance creates its sense of dread from things that seem pretty harmless, including employee handbooks, bizarre corporate perks, and meaningless everyday tasks at work. The company controls its workers through strange rules, rituals, and the fact that the innies have no outside life instead of obvious violence. The more Mark and the others learn about Lumon, the more they also begin asking whether their innies are separate people with lives and rights of their own. Given the show’s unique premise, it’s no surprise that it became Apple TV’s most-watched show during Season 2. It feels like a modern classic because it takes the most ordinary frustrations of working life and makes them feel existential in a way that no other show has.

blocks.x: Apple TV entered the streaming wars in 2019, which is pretty late compared to giants including Netflix and Amazon Prime. The platform had to build itself from scratch without decades of TV history behind it, but that’s what made its rise especially fascinating. Apple TV grew its reputation one series at a time. Some became immediate hits while others took a bit longer to find their audience. However, the common thread was that every show on the streamer knew what it wanted to be.

These titles never chased trends. Instead, they fully committed to their own unique worlds, characters, and ideas, and trusted audiences to follow along. A few years later, that consistency has left Apple TV with an unusually strong catalog of shows that already feel like they will go down in history. Here is a list of 10 such shows on the platform that have quietly become modern classics, not long after they premiered.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/pachinko-ji-hye-lee.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1

blocks.x: Image via Apple TV+

Pachinko tells its story across decades, but the way its time periods flow into each other is the heart of the story. The series follows Sunja, played in her younger years by Minha Kim and later in life by Yuh-Jung Youn, who is born in Korea under Japanese colonial rule. Her life changes after she becomes involved with the wealthy and mysterious Hansu (Lee Min-ho). The choices that follow eventually take her to Japan, where she is forced to build a life in a country that often treats Koreans like outsiders. Decades later, her grandson Solomon (Jin Ha) is living a completely different life in 1989 as he works in finance and tries to prove himself in a society his family once struggled to survive in.

Pachinko’s intimate storytelling makes it more than just a historical drama. Sunja and Solomon are separated by generations, but the show constantly reveals how much of his life has been shaped by her decisions. The poverty, discrimination, migration, and compromises that defined Sunja’s generation do not disappear, but just take different forms once the family becomes more successful. The show doesn’t make this contrast feel too on the nose, but quietly demonstrates how progress doesn’t always erase the past. Pachinko is one of Apple TV’s most acclaimed dramas because it unfolds on a massive historical scale, but still feels like a deeply personal family story.

The show is deliberately patient about answering its biggest questions and spends long stretches showing Carol test the limits of this strange new world she is suddenly in. If something does not make sense, she keeps digging until she understands how it works, even if that means inviting danger. Every episode of Silo expands the central character’s investigation to reveal the secrets of this underground community going back centuries. items.text:
Doctors have confirmed it: It's physically impossible for me to turn my nose up at a mecha action game. But despite this dire prognosis, I've been suspicious of Gundam Rogue Orbit—Bandai Namco's mobile suit action game coming in spring—since it was announced back in June.

The problem is the giant monsters. I'm a Gundam traditionalist. Gundam, to me, isn't about fighting aliens—it's about traumatized child war pilots becoming so psychic that their brains explode. But this week, Bandai found a way to coax me off my high horse: With an extremely sick model kit.

items.author: Zack Zwiezen

items.text:
Dan Houser helped write and produce every Grand Theft Auto as well as Red Dead Redemption 2. He was president of creative at Rockstar Games, the company he co-founded with his brother Sam Houser, at the time he left in 2020. He’s now working on new projects, including a comedic open-world game, and says he can’t watch the GTA 6 gameplay reveal because it would “distract” him creatively.

In a new podcast interview with Variety, Houser admitted that despite his connection with the Grand Theft Auto franchise and the fact that his brother is still in charge of Rockstar Games, the former GTA writer has no idea what was shown in the GTA 6 gameplay reveal that premiered in August on Netflix.

“I haven’t seen it yet,” said Houser. “I will try and avoid it because I always try and avoid stuff that’s going to distract or disrupt me creatively. And given that I spend a large amount of time trying to make open-world games, and the rest of my conscious time trying to figure out innovative ways to market them, I don’t need to see what other people are [doing]. I’m always trying to think about new ways of doing it, not sit there in some kind of comparison of what I would have done differently.”

Houser further explained that he can’t really play open-world games anymore because he ends up deconstructing how the game was made, and it distracts him too much.

“I find when I play them, I can almost deconstruct the strengths and weaknesses of the team in real time, and it’s distracting,” said Houser. “I’m always thinking, ‘Well, their animation team is weak, but I think this game design is fantastic.’ And, ‘Oh, I can imagine that meeting when they discuss this feature.’ I’m not a game designer; I’m a sort of creative director. So I’m trying to always find new things that haven’t been done before, or that I can steal from older media, quite frankly, or just inspired me, or things I always thought about.”

The former Rockstar Games head writer explained that “thankfully” he’s never needed to “be the person that understands what everyone else is doing,” so he doesn’t need to play all the new open-world games. Instead, other people at his new company, Absurd Ventures, founded in 2023, play all the new open-world games that come out for him.

“I’m trying to think about new ways of doing it,” said Houser.

“So when we worked on Red Dead Redemption, as soon as we started working, I never watched another Western. I never watched The Sopranos until after I left Rockstar. I saw one episode, because my girlfriend-now-wife and I did watch the finale in real time. I’d not seen any of it before that moment. And then I watched it all during COVID. And I’m grateful. It’s so good that it would have disrupted everything I did on GTA had I watched at the time. So I really try and avoid things that I think are going to overly influence me.”

As for what Houser is working on now, he is building out a few different multimedia franchises via Absurd Ventures. So far, the company has only released audio dramas, comic books, and novels. But it’s also developing two video games based on these media franchises.

“One is an open-world comedy which is trying to really lean into comedy and character memory, and that we’ll have more information on in the next few months,” said Houser. “And the other is a dystopian sci-fi about a video game development gone very wrong, and about a rogue AI that discovered sentience. But unfortunately, it was made by two people that didn’t like each other, so it doesn’t like itself.”

items.title: My Patience With Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave Is Wearing Dangerously Thin
items.author: Ash Parrish

items.text:
I’ve been playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave for two weeks now and the experience has started to take its toll. The world-building is entertaining and intriguing, representing a bold new direction for the sword-and-sorcery strategy RPG. But after thirty hours, the desire to know what’s going on and to discover the ultimate fates of these well-written, colorful characters is really the only things compelling me to continue playing the game.

The game’s character progression and EXP grind—at least in part one—are borderline tedious. Instead of reveling in a world replete with mystery and anachronisms, I’m spinning my wheels, wasting valuable time criss-crossing a map with precious little to show for my investment.

Fortune’s Weave works in roughly the same way as previous Fire Emblem games. Each of the four Flame Lords’ stories is broken up into parts. And despite my best efforts to focus on Theodora and make progress, I haven’t made it out of part one yet. Theodora is a queen newly enthroned, winning her crown after a fight with her brother cost her one of her arms. After securing a new, more powerful magic arm, Theodora has come to the Heroic Games to win back ancestral lands her kingdom has lost in the past. But as she fights her way through the tournament, she must also must fight against the corruption spreading from her newfound arm that’s slowly eroding her mind.

The character work in Fortune’s Weave is carrying the entire game. It’s not often you get to play queens in video games, and the royalty you do see is often portrayed as arrogant, cruel, and short-sighted. Whenever I’m watching or reading something with that kind of all-powerful authority figure, I always think, “I could do better. It’s so easy to do better.” When I play Theodora, she’s the “better” I think of. If it weren’t for the truly delightful support conversations between her and the crew she slowly amasses over time, I’d have put this game down long ago.

The way Fortune’s Weave handles time is at the heart of the painful acknowledgement that this game is not yet what I’ve been hoping for. There are still days with a calendar to manage, but they’re broken up into smaller time segments that become like a currency you spend whenever you move across the map or complete specific tasks. For example, going from 3/15 to 3/20 represents 20 time segments in addition to five concrete days. On paper, that sounds great; you have more “time” to do activities. The problem is you’re gonna be spending the majority of that time walking on the map.

Unlike in Three Houses where activities like training or cooking a meal would cost you time and advance the day, those are free in Fortune’s Weave. Again, sounds like a great deal, although you do “pay” for activities with a stamina meter for each character and artificial limits on how often you can complete an activity within a given day or week. Where you pay for your time is through map exploration, and the way the map is constructed…is bullshit.

When you want to move between destinations, you have to select your route in increments of one “time” segment at a time. There’s no option to pick a destination and automatically deduct how much time it’ll take to get there, likely because there are so many intersecting routes representing multiple ways to reach the same place. The map is littered with nodes that you can search for raw materials—fish, meat, vegetables, smithing materials—while on your way to wherever you’re going, in addition to dungeons (which are also bullshit) and towns where you can share a meal or buy goods.

What’s so frustrating is that the map is huge. If I want to explore a new area, I have to spend 15-20 chunks of time just to get there, another 15-20 to unlock an area’s nodes, then another 15-20 to get back. The game is generous, with some chapters offering over 100 chunks of time before your next deadline, but this is where the second frustration, character progression, comes in.

You can only train your party’s skills once a week and only in the main city. If I’m out and about exploring a big chunk of the map and decide I want to level my characters, I have to stop what I’m doing and head back to the main city, my chunks of time slipping away like grains of sand in an hourglass. Then, I have to spend that much time again, heading back to pick up where I left off. There are carriages you can use that can cut down some of that back and forth but they only work within an area, not between them.

I enjoyed the time management gameplay mechanic that undergirds The Blood of Dawnwalker, because there was narrative tension there. In Fortune’s Weave, it impedes rather than enhances. If I could train outside the main city, I’d hate this system a lot less. Thankfully, I know that after I pass some as-yet-undiscovered progression point, I’ll unlock fast travel. It can’t come soon enough.

Another frustrating component is how progression is gated. Certain sections of the map are blocked by gates only passable at a certain level of renown. You earn renown by participating in main story quests as well as completing general side quests and special side quests specific to each Flame Lord. In Theodora’s case, that means sending supplies to your citizens back home. You also need higher levels of renown if you want to widely recruit any one of the many colorful allies Fortune’s Weave throws at you. General side quests earn you a pittance. The best way, at least in part one, to earn the renown needed to grow your party and expand the map is by gathering supplies.

And it fucking sucks. You have to gather 10, 20, 30 pieces of a specific material from a specific region, and whether you even get what you need when you go looking is down to random chance. I just feel stuck on this unsatisfying wheel of walking across a map picking vegetables and fish like some kind of hobo hunter-gatherer. I am a Flame Lord, damnit! I’m supposed to be leading my troops from winged horseback, and I don’t even get to do that often enough!

Clashes in dungeons feel like a waste of time, trading blows back and forth with little friction or difficulty, and the strategic combat encounters that play out on a map are few and far between. And that double sucks because those battles are the only place you can really gain the kind of EXP you need to grow your characters. The other way is by sending your characters out on “auto activities” where they can either train, search for materials, or fight. I want to play the game! I don’t want it to play itself for me, but it’s felt like it’s on auto pilot for so much of my initial time with it, a constant cycle of explore and train, train and explore. The fact that this tedium is split across four characters makes experiencing everybody’s story feel like an insurmountable task. I don’t have the strength to sit through three more boring-ass part ones. I know there are boons you can accrue that are supposed to smooth out parallel playthroughs, but I haven’t seen them in action yet. And because of the way this game is structured, my first playthrough with the Flame Lord I love the most is the one that I’ll have the worst experience with, which I hate. If I had known this was going to be such a slog, I woulda picked Dietrich as the sacrificial struggle bus.

I don’t want it to play itself for me, but it’s felt like it’s on auto pilot for so much of my initial time with it, a constant cycle of explore and train, train and explore. The fact that this tedium is split across four characters makes experiencing everybody’s story feel like an insurmountable task. I don’t have the strength to sit through three more boring-ass part ones. I know there are boons you can accrue that are supposed to smooth out parallel playthroughs, but I haven’t seen them in action yet. And because of the way this game is structured, my first playthrough with the Flame Lord I love the most is the one that I’ll have the worst experience with, which I hate. If I had known this was going to be such a slog, I woulda picked Dietrich as the sacrificial struggle bus.

items.author: Amelia Zollner

items.text:
Something weird has been happening over the past few days. The social media platform X is obviously no stranger to spawning weird gaming trends that are partly or even wholly fueled by generative AI, like the proliferation of games about finding a needle in a haystack, but I’ve never been quite as exhausted by the algorithm-fueled slop as I am by a new plague of vibe-coded gaming mashups. Seemingly overnight, my entire homepage has somehow been taken over by modders who have used AI to develop unexpected crossovers that put famous games like Super Mario 64 inside of other famous games like Elden Ring.

Suddenly, my feed is filled with empty promises that have magically earned thousands of likes and millions of views.

Hey, you can fight Elden Ring bosses with a Minecraft sword!

Or with Mario!

You can shoot Skyrim NPCs with Escape from Tarkov guns!

You can now go skateboarding with Skate 3-style mechanics in Modern Warfare 2!

Not enough layers for you? You can even play the MW2 Skate 3 mod inside of Minecraft!

All of the above mods are AI-generated (or seem to be, in the case of the Tarkov mod, which was turned around in just a few hours after its creator noticed the trend).

There’s also this “every old Nintendo game” monstrosity, which was made by using AI to try to decompile a bunch of Nintendo DS–era games and then mash them back together into a Frankenstein’s monster fever dream of cozy slop in which you own a dog from Nintendogs and play minigames directly ripped from Cooking Mama while working a shift at Animal Crossing: New Leaf’s The Roost (it also allegedly involves other games including Reel Fishing 3, Story of Seasons, and Kingdom Hearts…somehow).

Most of these mods don’t seem to be downloadable yet (and solely exist as Twitter clips, likely uploaded in a rush right after Claude finished churning out its work), and we haven’t been able to verify that all of these are actually playable mods. I was, however, able to test out a Claude-coded mod that adds Minecraft’s items to Skyrim by modder chasmlol, whose Discord server has become somewhat of a hub for this sudden AI modding craze. I did not have a lot of fun with it!

I was a little tickled to find out I could actually break some parts of Skyrim‘s environment to obtain blocks, but after mining about two blocks from a mountain, I instantly fell through and got stuck amid some missing blocks with some awfully funky geometry. Some of these blocks were improperly assigned, too—breaking a metal gate gave me wood—and others failed to render at all. And then, before I even had a chance to dive into battle, I got stuck behind an invisible wall that definitely does not exist in regular Skyrim!

I get that this is an early version of the mod, and I know it’s going to be buggy. But even if it were polished and entirely bug-free, its design does so little to actually integrate the two games into each other that it would still just feel like a sandbox meant to generate viral Twitter clips rather than anything that could result in an actual playthrough of Skyrim using Minecraft’s items. My inventory (shown through Minecraft‘s usual HUD, which shamelessly covered up Skyrim‘s subtitles) came packed with diamond tools, a full set of iron armor, and even a few golden apples, all resources that are fairly difficult to get in Minecraft but were given to me literally right off the bat. The mod comes with a crafting table, sure, but I have no idea how one might actually obtain the resources needed to craft most items—you can’t actually go mining because the stone layer under the world is only a few blocks deep and seemingly ore-free, and I failed to come across any natural food sources, either.

The rest of these mods seem similarly slipshod. I can’t figure out how on earth Tarkov gear in that other Skyrim mod is obtained or how to actually score points while doing kickflips inside of MW2 and maybe also inside of Minecraft (or what said points might get you if they actually existed). None of these mechanics actually synergize with each other in a way that means anything!

Minecraft, Elden Ring, Nintendogs, and all of the other games that have been melded into each other over and over throughout the past few days are special because of the design decisions that were made during their development. Their systems are tightly intertwined and were designed to feed into each other, which is why ripping out parts of these games, unceremoniously smashing them together, and failing to do any real design work to integrate their mechanics or add any semblance of originality results in some incredibly incohesive and unplayable mods.

It’s novel to see one of these clips come across your feed for a few seconds, I guess, but none of these mods have created anything that even resembles the actual gameplay they promise. Sure, you can post your cool skateboard trick appended to an MW2 trickshot to score an easy thousand likes. But does anyone actually want to play these things?

items.title: RetroSpace offers a huge sci-fi playground for inquisitive space janitors, but I'm not that System Shocked by the tools at your disposal
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot
items.text:
In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right.

The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar.

In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind.

Watch on YouTube

RetroSpace takes place aboard Aurora 5, a pseudo-1970s interstellar ark that has tumbled into a black hole, and somehow come away with a mild case of temporal indecision – certain areas flip between timeframes - rather than spaghettification and incomprehensible doom. You are a janitor, woken from cryo to find a lot of stuff on fire, a lot of people dead, and a lot of other people deranged and monsterfied by gene-modding. Taking up your power wrench, you set out for the habitat hub and soon become embroiled in missions assigned by a handful of coherent survivors, including a sentient AI and a talking pig fellah.

These take you out to the far corners of the space station, which is very much the main character here. There's a "garden" sector that consists of a verdant silo with a starry dome, its spiral stairs and crawlspaces leading down to what I think is a bubbling soup of fertiliser. There's a train that circles the whole facility – not a camouflaged loading screen, as with chapter breaks in Dead Space, but an actual monorail car that travels in real time. There are a lot of audiologs, hackable terminals, and comedy public safety signs or adverts. As you might expect from the devisers of chicken detective games, RetroSpace skews toward caricature, which can get obnoxious – there's an audiolog early on that pokes fun at NPCs who leave scary audiologs. Still, it feels like the devs are fundamentally committed to making an engrossing world.

There's a persistent mystique woven around the station's janitors. Propaganda posters cast you and your lost brethren as urban legends, seldom seen by regular folk because you're always up a ladder or behind a bulkhead doing whatever it is you helmeted weirdos do with those sprays and spanners. Each sector has a locked or concealed utility closet with a portal to the Janitor's Haven - an interdimensional hideaway set up by union organisers, where you'll hang out with story-critical NPCs and do the bulk of your upgrading and customising.

If the station is a peach, I'm a little less convinced so far by the tools at your disposal. On the one hand, you've got weapons such as pistols, shotguns, and rayguns, all (eventually) upgradeable. On the other, you've got more indirect or tactical accessories such as cloaking devices, computer-hacking gizmos, and propulsive fire extinguishers. On the third hand, you've got genetic engineering or Mutamods, which range from giving yourself grasshopper thighs for higher jumping, moth ears so that you heal in light, or biceps full of rhino DNA for meatier clobbering.

The gene-modding cuts both ways: when you die, you'll be cloned for free at the nearest Bacta tank equivalent, but you'll be saddled with a random cartoon affliction for your troubles. I came away from one misadventure with a body prone to uncontrollable sneezing and swearing, which did not help with subsequent attempts at stealth. Fortunately, you can purge the debuffs by siphoning genetic material from the nearest vanilla human corpse, and Aurora 5 has no shortage of those.

Within the world, you can also do things like hold up crates to block bullets, or spray paths of water to create an electricity trap before smacking a circuit box. It's all entertaining enough, but many of the ideas are overly familiar from System Shock, Bioshock and Arkane's Prey. I'm really hoping that somewhere in RetroSpace, there lurks a tool or combination of tools that is as daft in its own way as Prey's Mimic ability. Or the slapstick bullshit you get in Skin Deep.

As it is, I'm finding that I'm too often just shooting enemies because I'm unexcited by the more devious ways of avoiding or defeating them. The enemies have their moments – lop a bugman's head off, and it might sprout legs, while the manpigs are drawn to trails of blood - but a lot of the time, they're just awareness indicators you can either avoid or gun down.

If you're comfortable with how comfortable RetroSpace can feel, as a love letter to certain famous immersive sims, you'll likely be able to forgive all this. Myself, I'd say the station ambience and secretive level design are worth the occasional sense of deja-vu. I'll keep plugging on with the game, though games journalism being what it currently is, I sadly don't have time for a full review. Find out more about RetroSpace on Steam. Let me know if you spot any really sexy airvents.

items.title: Adult Swim’s “Get Jiro” Serves Up Bloody, Sloppy Culinary Revenge
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One,
items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

items.text:
To most, the highlight of this week's big Deadlock patch is the snazzy map makeover, new heroes, and tons of quality-of-life additions. To me, it's all about the patch notes.

I spend a lot of waking hours reading white-text-on-black-background changelogs in this line of work, so when a page comes along that was specifically designed to be pleasant and exciting, it deserves to be rewarded. Valve has a long history of designing beautiful, bespoke webpages to introduce meaningful changes to its games, but the graphics department is really going ballistic with Deadlock.

ValveValveValveValve

(Image credit: Valve)

(Image credit: Valve)The City Never Sleeps patch notes are styled like a tourism brochure for Deadlock's refreshed New York City, walking readers through scenic stops across the four major districts (Chinatown, Theater, Haunted Lot, and Plaza). Descriptions weave between in-world storytelling and technical explanation where it makes sense, with Valve's splashes of humor reminding readers not to take any of this too seriously.

(Image credit: Valve)Dotted lines draw the reader to new points of interest as they scroll while furthering the map motif, and the page is stuffed with custom artwork for new items and mechanics that might only exist there. Valve did such an annoyingly good job with presenting the next era of Deadlock that I'm almost tempted to play a MOBA (but only almost).

Finally, some good food. Welcome back, Valve patch notes.

Valve's golden age of patch notes

September 30, 2010: The Mann-conomy Update (Image credit: Valve)It cannot be understated that Valve pioneered storytelling in multiplayer shooters with Team Fortress 2, arguably kicking off with the 2009 WAR! Update, aka "Soldier vs. Demo." This was before the concept of multiplayer games having seasons, before League of Legends had a TV show, before "live service" was even a thing—Valve had created a cast of nine lovable weirdos and new updates that weren't just dropping items, but telling stories that put the characters in conflict with one another and added context to the multiplayer maps we'd already been fighting in for two years.

It was weird in the first place for an FPS to receive so many free post-launch additions, and it was even weirder for a developer to treat the arrival of new weapons, modes, and hats as worthy of dedicated splash pages with accompanying comic books.

TF2 was the gold standard for post-launch support, and its patch notes drew massive interest, often dropping late on a Thursday or Friday, Pacific time, hinting that Valve may have been polishing until the last minute. Valve's blog posts were never the same month-to-month, often adopting new color schemes, layouts, and original elements for the occasion.

February 24, 2009: The Scout Update (Image credit: Valve)July 8, 2010: The Engineer UpdateValveJune 27, 2012: PyromaniaValveFebruary 24, 2009: The Scout UpdateValveDecember 17, 2009: WAR! UpdateValveThere was no single template they stuck to. The Engineer update introduced his advanced Gunslinger gauntlet and Wrangler as blueprints with hand-written notes, while Scout's update debuted the Force-A-Nature scattergun in a department store catalog. I especially love announcing the Mac version of TF2 with a white, sanitized home page complete with symmetrical boxes and tiny text in the style of Apple circa 2002.

June 10, 2010: The Mac Update (Image credit: Valve)Poring over the "history" section of the TF2 website in 2026 is like uncovering one of those lost civilizations that invented a ton of sophisticated things before everyone else.

April 14, 2011: The Hatless Update (Image credit: Valve)We're in an era marked by formulaic seasons, videogames as advertisement platforms, and teams scrambling to alter plans when they're not immediately popular. And yet 15 years ago, Valve had so much confidence in its direction that it could decide to wage a war between Soldier and Demoman one day (live-tracking the kills between both classes—Soldier narrowly won with 6.40M kills to the collective Demomen's 6.37M), introduce a crafting system the next, and then rebrand as Scream Fortress for October.

It wasn't exclusively good vibes—Valve caught flak for its (now quaint) paid hats, paid loot boxes, and speculative marketplace that became a fixture of updates. In a move that I would be surprised to see a studio make today, Valve made fun of itself at the time with a subsequent "Hatless Update".

Deadlock's blogs are practically retro, it feels weird to say. I wonder what inspired Valve to go this hard again. Counter-Strike 2 and Dota 2's changelogs do not share the same sense of theater. Their patch notes are comparatively regular, functional bullet lists—perhaps in line with how often those games are updated. Valve does occasionally produce unique web pages for major CS2 announcements or Dota 2 events, but we're far from the days when an incremental Mann VS Machine update was announced with a lavish movie poster in the style of kaiju cinema.

December 20, 2012: The Mecha Update (Image credit: Valve)TF2's exceptional, ever-changing patch notes were a reflection of the game they promoted. Valve leveraged the flexibility of an arena shooter and imagined a world where Red and Blu were real factions locked in stupid conflicts. You never really knew what elaborate scenarios Valve would think up next for its over-the-top action figures, and that filled TF2 fans with a sense of wonder that very few games have pulled off since. Maybe it's no coincidence that the only example of innovative multiplayer storytelling in recent years, Helldivers 2, is another over-the-top war game that finds comedy in the futility of endless violence.

Valve is tapping into that dormant TF2 energy in small ways with Deadlock, and it's great, though I wonder if, being a MOBA, the game's inherent sweat level will eventually lead to a regimented, low-nonsense future that's more focused on the minutiae of balance. Whatever Deadlock is up to years from now, I'll be keeping up with the patch notes.

items.author: andy.chalk@pcgamer.com (Andy Chalk)

items.text:
I don't typically have much love for billion-dollar corporations dropping the 'meet our legal department' hammer on no-budget modders who are just trying to exercise their creative muscles, but in this one instance I'm willing to let it slide: Bethesda has issued a cease-and-desist order to an "AI creator" who made a Fallout game set in New York City that runs in browsers.

That's actually overstating it: As Chris First explained in his X feed (via RPS), he "directed Claude and a studio of AI agents" to make the game for him. Nor was there any new creative thought injected into the process, First continued, saying he asked for a game that was "not inspired by" Fallout, but that was "exactly like Fallout."

This is the result.

Fallout: New York, a full Fallout game you play in your browser, built with Claude Opus 5.5.Quests. Dialogue trees. V.A.T.S. A working Pip-Boy.Zero texture files. Zero sound files. Every building, weapon, face and sound is generated by code. pic.twitter.com/58Vls0mOYxSeptember 28, 2026

I know that being playable in a browser is a limiting factor, but this is really just something I'd rather not play at all. It stands in such sharp contrast to mods like Fallout: London or Skyblivion, efforts that reflect genuine passion, commitment, and creativity—and yes, those mods are massive undertakings that require years of effort from hundreds of volunteers, but they also don't suck and I feel like maybe there's a lesson to be learned there.

Anyway, whether I want to play it or not is now a moot point, because yesterday First said he received a message from ZeniMax Media telling him to knock it off—specifically, that the domain name he registered for the project, fallout.nyc, infringes on the studio's IP rights.

(Image credit: Chris First (Twitter))I don't know if First was expecting sympathy for his plight, but he doesn't seem to be getting much of it. Some responses criticize him for calling the project "Fallout," which is just about daring Bethesda to do something, but there's also plenty of heat over the use of AI to make the thing. A few optimists suggest First would be fine if he just changed the name, but he doesn't seem inclined to pursue that course.

That's probably for the best: Maybe I'm being overly harsh here (although I don't think so) but the one clear drawback to that plan is that changing the name doesn't change the fact that it looks like garbola. Playing a low-poly Fallout in a browser isn't an especially impressive technical feat—you can do the same with Morrowind, and it actually looks like Morrowind—and if you just want some really cheap Fallout, Fallout 3 is $2.49 in the Steam Autumn Sale, or you can snag New Vegas for a fiver.

I do sympathize with First's urge for a proper new Fallout game: I'm a little tired of the formula, but it's been 11 years since Fallout 4 and that's too damn long. But this ain't it, as the kids say, and while I'm never going to sign up for the corporate cheerleading squad, I can't say I'm sorry to see this one consigned to the dustbin, where it belongs.

items.title: Possible Love is an excellent layoff movie, and an alarming recession indicator
items.author: Monica Castillo
items.summary: Lee Chang-dong’s layered drama Possible Love, running the festival circuit before hitting Netflix in November, is a movie for now. Following the intricate
items.text:
Lee Chang-dong’s layered drama Possible Love, running the festival circuit before hitting Netflix in November, is a movie for now. Following the intricate pains and desires of two couples whose lives intersect for the shooting of a documentary, the Burning filmmaker’s new movie is about rising economic unease, class divisions, and how it all affects people. It’s also one of the most poignant recent depictions of the grief that comes from losing one’s job, and the fallout that comes with it—all of which, sadly, feels all too relatable for many around the world.


Lee follows Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who was laid off from his longtime employer, and his wife Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon). As she steps up to help the family in a new factory, they meet documentarian Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her entrepreneur husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), who want to feature the couple’s story in Ye-ji’s latest project about layoffs from corporate restructuring. Their lives become intertwined as first Mi-ok then Ho-seok share their experiences of his lob loss. They become so entangled in each other’s lives, in fact, that the line between documentarian and subject starts to blur.


﻿﻿


More than just a plot point for Possible Love, the grief Ho-seok and Mi-ok share is carefully presented and deeply felt. Mi-ok is more forthcoming about her emotions and memories, sharing her experience of solidarity and support in the wake of the layoffs among fellow laid-off employees, as well as the social excommunication she felt after her husband’s job was cut. She explains their life changes in both major and less noticeable ways: Not only did she have to get a job at a different factory while her husband looked for work, but Ho-seok’s carefully carved marble table outside their home never got to welcome any parties after he lost the means to host gatherings.


Through conversations for the film-within-the-film, the couple unpack their pain, shame, guilt, and sometimes overwhelming grief that can only be greeted with tears over the loss of identity, purpose, and means to provide for their families, including the couple’s young son. In one of Possible Love‘s most tense moments, the distant father follows one of his still-employed ex-colleagues who’s buying a birthday cake for their child, the same he was doing for his son. But he follows them further, going to the restaurant where they’re celebrating with a hearty meal and, eventually, the nice cake. He-seok sulks in the shadow of his former life, a ghost only another waiter seems to notice. In group therapy sessions, other workers share similar experiences lamenting their former lives. They felt like they were treated like the walking dead, compared to their still-employed counterparts they considered “the living.” Through no fault of their own, they not only lost their livelihood, they lost something representative of life.


Although America may not officially be in a recession, that hasn’t eased the overall economic fears of many after so many have been affected by the waves of recent layoffs because of corporate restructuring, mergers and acquisitions, and the fears around whatever the looming threat of AI will do to the workforce. South Korea, like the United States, has also weathered a number of high-profile layoffs, including the devastating round that inspired Lee to start working on the script for Possible Love. At a Q&A at the New York Film Festival, Lee said he developed the character of the documentarian in order to explore their experiences, because even he was unsure if he would be the right one to tell that kind of story.


﻿


This isn’t the first time a crummy economy, job insecurity, and rampant unemployment has made its way into the pictures. Back in the days of the Great Depression, comedies like Sullivan’s Travels, It Happened One Night, and My Man Godfrey touched on the issues of the time, acknowledging the hardships many in the audience were experiencing, but with a glamorous sense of escapism. Even the Mervyn LeRoy/Busby Berkeley musical Gold Diggers Of 1933 can’t escape the realistic struggle of its tenuously employed chorus girls, whose shows are closed by the bank faster than they can open to audiences. A drama like Frank Borzage’s Man’s Castle dove deeper into the insecurity shouldered by Spencer Tracy’s character as he tries to help a fellow unemployed love interest, but he’s afraid of married family life because he can’t guarantee that he can afford it.


Another wave of layoff movies welled up after the 2008 financial crisis. Downsizing became the enemy of the people in movies like Up In The Air and The Company Men. Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Tokyo Sonata followed a laid-off worker so riddled with shame, he hid his firing from his family and proceeded to continue commuting to keep up appearances. While today’s financial pressures have not sunk as deeply as those in the late aughts, Possible Love is the second major Korean release in recent years to take on the topic. Last year, Park Chan-wook’s dark comedy No Other Choice, took a satirical look at a desperate character, Man-su (Lee Byung-hun), who loses his job after 25 years of service. While his family makes do without certain luxuries, and weighs the possibility of losing their home, Man-su takes matters into his own hands, literally eliminating the competition for a shot at the next job that comes up.


While unemployment and layoffs are sometimes the starting dramatic premise or a mere punchline in some movies, Possible Love arrives at the story already in progress. What stands out is not just the act of losing one’s job, but the emotional toll that comes after. Informed by Lee’s interviews with people who have experienced layoffs, it’s a movie that takes its time to sit with these characters and gives them space to process their feelings, perhaps for the first time. The couple’s pent-up feelings of betrayal and abandonment eventually break out, especially as the interviews probe further, acknowledging the depth with which these corporate decisions have real-life lasting effects. Possible Love is a reminder to listen to these stories and sit with those in pain and grief, because the experience of losing one’s work, identity, and community all at once can be crushingly isolating and so much more complicated than a separation agreement.
